entry.title: A Design Checklist You Can Give Your AI
entry.content:
I wanted a link I could paste into an AI conversation and say: use this to check the interface, explain what needs work, and suggest fixes.

I assembled Design Guide for AI around that idea. It includes 138 checklists and 908 individual items from Checklist Design, with instructions for choosing the relevant checks and reporting what the agent can verify.

Give the agent a starting point

Open the guide page, copy the review prompt, and add your website, screenshots, or project files. The assistant needs access to the interface as well as the guide.

For a shorter prompt, use:

Read https://jienweng.github.io/design/llms.txt and follow its review protocol. Review this interface using the relevant checklists. Account for every selected item, cite evidence, and separate observed problems from checks you cannot verify. Suggest fixes before changing anything.

Then add the interface you want reviewed. You can narrow the request to a screen, component, or flow: “Review this sign-up form” gives the agent a clearer scope than “Check my app.”

The LLM entry point contains the review instructions and links to individual checklists. An agent can fetch the ones it needs. The complete text guide contains the whole collection for offline use or an assistant that cannot follow the individual links. If it cannot open links at all, paste the relevant text into the conversation.

What the agent should return

Before reviewing, the agent should explain which checklists it selected and why. A form might need the input-field, button, submission, and validation checklists. A screenshot of an empty state calls for a different selection.

Each selected item gets a status: Present, Partial, Missing, Not applicable, or Unverified. The report should include the evidence and location, then propose fixes for observed problems. It also has to reconcile its item counts and list anything it skipped.

For example, a screenshot can show that an email field has no visible label. It cannot establish how a screen reader announces the field. The report should separate those observations and say what test is still needed.

The same applies to optional elements. A checklist might mention an illustration, but a small utility form may have no use for one. The agent should explain that decision rather than recommend adding decoration to satisfy a list.

Where the checklists come from

Checklist Design publishes an official agent-skill repository under the MIT license. I used its published bundle rather than scrape the website page by page.

The checklist items, descriptions, and tips are their work. I added the website presentation, shareable text files, review protocol, and checks for incomplete reports. The license and source manifest identify the original authors and the pinned source commit.

The collection covers design systems, web apps, mobile apps, websites, and user flows. It is a snapshot; future changes to the source need to be reviewed and imported.

What I tested

I ran three fresh agent reviews with different evidence: a form’s source code, an empty-state screenshot, and a modal’s source plus recorded browser observations. The reviewers were not given the expected answers.

Across their selected checklists, they reported all 37 items and matched the expected outcomes in 19 checks. They found the four planted problems: a missing field label, missing supporting text, no modal close action, and a modal that overflowed on mobile. They left unseen behavior unverified and respected the request to omit decorative illustrations.

These were three controlled cases using one model. They do not establish how every model will handle a large product or an ambiguous screenshot. The report validator checks item IDs, missing rows, totals, and completion claims. Someone still needs to assess whether the evidence supports the findings and whether the suggested fixes help.

To try it, copy the prompt from the guide and start with one screen or flow you can inspect yourself.

entry.title: The Maths Behind PolyArb
entry.content:
PolyArb looks for Polymarket YES and NO shares that together cost less than USD 1 after fees. The first calculation fits on one line. Deciding how much to buy takes more work, because the displayed prices may cover only a few shares, fees can reduce the shares received, and the two orders can fill differently.

This post explains the general mathematics behind the PolyArb project. The source code is not publicly shared. All prices and trading outcomes below are hypothetical. They are examples for checking the arithmetic, not results from a live run.

Why a pair is worth USD 1

Take a binary market and let its YES payout be $X$. The complementary NO payout is $1-X$. Holding one of each gives

$$ X+(1-X)=1. $$

The shares must belong to the same condition and form a complete complementary set. Buying YES on one question and NO on a similar question does not establish this identity. Polymarket's portfolio documentation describes merging a matching pair back into collateral.

For equal quantities $q$, ignoring fees and other costs, buying at prices $p_Y$ and $p_N$ gives the profit

$$ \pi(q)=q(1-p_Y-p_N). $$

Suppose YES costs USD 0.46 and NO costs USD 0.51. Buying 100 of each costs USD 97. The complete set has a USD 100 payout, leaving a gross USD 3 spread. This calculation assumes both quantities are acquired at those prices and the complete set can be converted or settled as expected.

Buy fees can leave fewer pairs than ordered

A useful first model subtracts a dollar fee from that USD 3. A model for fees deducted from received shares needs to account for the smaller net balances.

Let a hypothetical model use a fee rate $r$ and an exponent $e$ to calculate the dollar fee per gross share at price $p$ as

$$ f(p)=r[p(1-p)]^e. $$

This is a parameterised example. It should not be read as a universal fee schedule for every market. The market's applicable fee rules and parameters still need to be checked.

Converting the dollar fee into shares gives a retained fraction

$$ a(p)=1-\frac{f(p)}{p}. $$

If both orders buy $q$ gross shares at fixed prices, the net balances become $q,a(p_Y)$ and $q,a(p_N)$. The number of complete pairs is limited by the smaller balance:

$$ m=q\min{a(p_Y),a(p_N)}. $$

Valuing any unmatched remainder at zero gives a conservative paired profit, before other costs,

$$ \pi_{\mathrm{pair}}=m-q(p_Y+p_N). $$

Use the earlier prices and assume, only for this example, $r=0.02$ and $e=1$. Then

$$ a(0.46)=1-0.02(0.54)=0.9892, $$

$$ a(0.51)=1-0.02(0.49)=0.9902. $$

Orders for 100 shares on each side leave 98.92 YES shares and 99.02 NO shares. Only 98.92 pairs are covered by the complete-set calculation. Against the USD 97 purchase cost, that leaves USD 1.92 before other costs. There are also 0.10 unmatched NO shares; this bound assigns them no value.

For a range of possible fill prices, a conservative estimate can use the smallest retained fraction across that range. Fees and purchase costs must use consistent units.

The cheapest price may cover only a small order

Suppose the asks are:

SidePriceShares available at that price
YESUSD 0.4620
YESUSD 0.5080
NOUSD 0.51100

The first 20 pairs cost USD 0.97 each before fees. Buying 100 YES shares requires taking the next level too. The actual cost of buying 100 shares on both sides, if this book remains available, is

$$ C(100)=20(0.46)+80(0.50)+100(0.51)=100.20. $$

Even with no fees, the USD 100 paired payout would leave a USD 0.20 loss. Multiplying the best displayed prices by 100 would have reported a USD 3 profit.

A depth-aware calculation can evaluate quantities at depth breakpoints, subject to budget and size constraints. For a candidate size $q$, it finds the limit prices $L_Y(q)$ and $L_N(q)$ needed to reach that quantity. A conservative cost bound is

$$ C_{\max}(q)=q[L_Y(q)+L_N(q)]. $$

At $q=100$, this bound is USD 101. At $q=20$, it is USD 19.40. The bound charges every share at its leg's limit price, so it can exceed the cost calculated by walking the book.

A profitable plan still needs two fills

The cost and payout bounds assume both legs fill in the required quantities. They do not guarantee that execution will produce those balances.

Suppose the YES order fills for 100 shares but the NO order fills for only 30. Ignore fees here to isolate the quantity mismatch. The holdings can be written as

$$ 100Y+30N=30(Y+N)+70Y. $$

Thirty complete pairs have a USD 30 combined payout. The remaining 70 YES shares depend on the outcome or on the price available when they are sold. If the bot tries to complete the hedge, it may have to pay more for NO than the original plan allowed.

For arbitrary net balances $n_Y$ and $n_N$, the complete-pair quantity is $\min(n_Y,n_N)$. The unmatched quantity is $|n_Y-n_N|$. A record of submitted orders cannot establish either number; execution records must show what filled and what fees were deducted.

These bounds require fresh market data, matching token identities, and both fills. Stale data or a missing leg can invalidate a proposed trade.

From a price observation to an execution record

A technical workflow needs to preserve enough evidence to reconstruct each decision. Start with both order books for the same condition, their observation times, and the fee parameters used for the calculation. Reject a candidate if either book is too old under the chosen freshness policy.

Next, calculate an affordable quantity from executable depth and net shares after fees. Apply limits on order cost and unmatched exposure before submitting orders. A positive spread alone does not answer either question.

After submission, track each leg independently. Record the requested quantity, filled quantity, average fill price, deducted fees, and remaining order quantity. Reconcile those records against the resulting balances before counting complete pairs. An order acknowledgement confirms receipt of a request; it does not confirm a fill.

These are general design requirements for evaluating a paired-trade system. They do not describe or expose PolyArb's private implementation.

What I would check in a paper-trading result

PolyArb is now in production and also supports paper trading. This section concerns simulated results, not evidence of live returns. Paper trading uses real market prices and simulated orders, with balances that persist across restarts.

The dashboard helps inspect activity, but a detected price gap, a risk-approved decision, a simulated fill, and realised profit describe different stages. To assess a run, I would check which prices and quantities were observed, how old the book was, which fee parameters were used, and how the simulator decided that each order filled.

For a completed trade, the accounting should include the paired collateral actually recovered, proceeds or remaining value from unmatched shares, the purchase cost, and other execution costs. With consistent units, that is

$$ \pi_{\mathrm{net}}=M+U-C-K, $$

where $M$ is recovered paired collateral, $U$ is the unmatched inventory's proceeds or marked value, $C$ is the purchase cost, and $K$ covers additional costs not already deducted. If $U$ includes unsold inventory, part of this figure remains unrealised.

Before treating a paper balance as evidence of live profitability, I would compare its assumed fills with the depth and timestamps recorded for each leg. A simulator that grants both fills at the observed prices has already assumed away the execution failure in the previous example.

entry.title: Trying to Understand PaperTrade's Tokenomics
entry.content:
PaperTrade caught my attention because losing traders receive PAPER, which they can stake for USDC rewards. Someone could lose money on a trade and still come out ahead through the rewards. I wanted to understand how that works, where the USDC comes from, and why the next person would join.

The tokenomics give people more than one reason to trade. Some want to profit from price movements; others may accept trading losses to accumulate PAPER. The mint rate also changes over time, so an early participant and a later participant can pay the same amount in losses for different amounts of PAPER. That made me curious about who benefits as more people join, and whether the rewards can keep attracting activity once earning tokens becomes less generous.

To work through that, I needed to understand how the LP pays winners, how losses become tokens, and what stakers can claim. I also looked at the relayer because being able to close a position affects whether a trader can realize those outcomes.

I worked through these questions in a ChatGPT conversation, then checked the linked documentation and Guardian review. These notes cover the published design as of 21 October 2026. I haven't checked every deployed contract or reconstructed its live balances.

Who pays when you win?

PaperTrade uses Hyperliquid's prices to create synthetic trades against its own liquidity pool, or LP. It reads the best bid and ask and takes their midpoint. Your position doesn't become an order on Hyperliquid's perpetual order book. The LP takes the other side. The documentation describes BTC and ETH positions with multipliers up to 1,000×. Trading and pricing

Say you put $100 into a position at 100×. You now have $10,000 of exposure. If the price moves 0.5% in your direction, the linear gross profit is $50. PaperTrade applies an asymmetric impact adjustment to profitable closes, so that calculation alone doesn't tell you what gets credited. It also leaves out liquidation and the other settlement rules.

The LP needs USDC to pay that profit. PaperTrade's Martingaler mechanism allows the pool to start without upfront seed capital and build its bankroll from trading losses. If it cannot cover winning payouts, those payouts can wait. Martingaler overview

That was where I needed to slow down. A profitable trade can leave you waiting for money.

The documentation splits the accounting into three parts:

StateWhat it records
TreasuryTracked LP funds under the settlement rules
sideBucketProceeds parked while the payout queue is active
Payout queueUnpaid winning profits, with older claims paid first

On an ordinary winning close, your original margin returns to your available balance separately. Any profit that cannot be funded goes into the queue. Later backing can pay the claims through a harvest process. Solvency and queue

For a simplified example, suppose you're owed $5,000 of profit and only $1,000 can be paid immediately. The remaining $4,000 is still owed to you. Putting it in a queue doesn't create the missing USDC. You have to wait for backing to arrive.

Losing a trade earns PAPER

Eligible realized losses mint PAPER. The documented starting rate is 100 PAPER per dollar of eligible loss basis while tracked LP is below $2 million. After the threshold, the rate decays using a high-water mark. Distributing funds out of the LP doesn't reset it to the earlier rate. Mint curve

So the same eligible loss can earn different amounts of PAPER depending on when it happens. I say “eligible loss” because the mint basis can differ from the gross amount a trader loses under the settlement rules.

You can stake PAPER for a share of eligible USDC distributions. The standard documented staking model has no lockup or cooldown, and rewards can be claimed into the Exchange balance before withdrawal. Staking and claims

Suppose your stake stays at 1% of the pool while $50,000 is distributed. You would receive $500. But you still need to compare that with what you spent acquiring PAPER, and your share can shrink as other people stake. One distribution doesn't tell you how much the next one will pay.

This also changes how I would read the trading volume. Someone might trade because they expect BTC to rise. Someone else might accept a loss because they want PAPER. Both add volume, but they are doing different things.

Guardian identifies farming on gross losses, including hedged strategies, as a retained economic risk. A trader's losing position can qualify for tokens while another position offsets some of that loss. Guardian security review

The liquidation rule needs a separate read

PaperTrade has a hard-bust trigger. Liquidation through that path takes the full isolated margin, even where a voluntary close at the trigger could still return some equity. The documentation describes a buffer of roughly five basis points of price. Liquidations

With a large position relative to your margin, a small price difference can take a large share of your money. I wouldn't use the ordinary closing calculation to estimate what comes back after liquidation. The two paths follow different rules.

Who submits the trades?

The user signs an instruction, and the relayer and batch executor submit it to the Exchange. Session-key and contract checks validate the authority behind it. Architecture

I can inspect what reaches the contract. That still leaves me asking what happened to a request before it got there. Was it delayed? Rejected? Could I submit it another way?

Guardian's review records concerns about relayer dependence and price bounds on signed instructions. It also describes upgrade authority, while the off-chain relayer, sweeper, and keepers were outside the review's scope. I can't treat that contract review as proof that the submission service is fair or always available. Guardian security review

The protocol also documents a risk from using the instantaneous best-bid/ask midpoint. Changes to those quotes can affect its reference price. Open-interest caps and adjustments to winning PnL can limit exposure, but they don't remove the risk. Risk documentation

I also want to know how I would close my position if the authorized relayer stopped submitting requests. I'd want to see that fallback demonstrated.

Why would people join?

The reward design gives people a reason to arrive early. They can earn PAPER at the earlier mint rate, stake it, and potentially receive USDC. If they share those rewards, other people have a reason to look into it too.

That's how I read the incentive loop. I don't know the team's internal marketing plan. I also haven't verified the paid-promotion claims, launch figures, or wallet earnings discussed in the original chat, so I'm leaving them out.

What interests me is whether people keep trading when earning PAPER becomes less attractive. I would look at repeat participation after rewards decline, how concentrated the distributions are, and how much volume comes from identifiable farming. Counting wallets wouldn't be enough because one person can use several addresses.

entry.title: How I Define When a Payment Is Complete
entry.content:
I coordinate an engineering team working on Web3 payments. I maintain the backlog and roadmap, run Scrum ceremonies, and clarify priorities with the business owner.

When gathering requirements, I start with the intended users and how they will understand the flow. For a payment, I ask what the customer sees while waiting and whether the status tells them to wait, retry, or take another action.

When the merchant can credit a payment

“Make deposits more reliable” leaves a decision open: which event allows the merchant to credit its ledger?

I work through that boundary with the business owner and engineers. In the documented CryptoRails flow, the browser detects incoming funds and gives the customer feedback. The merchant backend credits the ledger after receiving and verifying the signed settlement webhook.

The trade-off is waiting for confirmation and server verification before calling the payment complete. The interface still needs to show progress during that wait. Treating detection as completion would let the screen promise an outcome the backend has yet to verify.

What I put into acceptance criteria

That boundary changes what the team has to test:

  • Deposit detection updates the interface without marking the payment settled.
  • A delayed confirmation leaves the payment pending.
  • The backend verifies the webhook before updating the ledger.
  • A repeated webhook or retry cannot credit the same payment twice.

A successful demo covers only one of these paths. I include the delayed and duplicate cases when defining done with the team.

Keeping the scope deliverable

The request also needs agreed networks, failure cases, and responses for the user. I turn those decisions into backlog items, track dependencies, and raise blocked work or competing requests with the business owner.

The CryptoRails workflow shows the deposit and consolidation sequence behind these requirements. Product-specific business details, internal metrics, and implementation details remain confidential.

Related reading

  • The CryptoRails deposit-to-settlement workflow.
  • Why a Web3 payment needs more than a transaction hash.

entry.title: TRON Energy Is a Product Requirement
entry.content:
On EVM networks, transactions normally need the network’s native coin for gas. TRON token transfers use Energy and may consume Bandwidth. If an account lacks Energy, a transfer can burn TRX to cover the shortfall.

That changes the payment cost and the checks required before broadcast.

The payment sequence

In our payment flow, we apply Energy rental before a resource-heavy TRON transaction:

  1. Validate the payment and network.
  2. Check the transaction’s resource requirement.
  3. Arrange rented Energy when needed.
  4. Broadcast and monitor the transaction.
  5. Wait for the required confirmation condition.
  6. Reconcile the transfer with the payment request.

Requirements and testing

The backlog needs to account for insufficient resources, rental failure, unexpected costs, and confirmation delays. QA also needs chain-specific address, wallet, and fee cases.

I now check these requirements before the team designs the error states. Exact rental rules and internal implementation details remain confidential.

entry.title: Why We Built an Internal CRM After Trying Salesforce
entry.content:
At Quandatics, I’m working on an internal CRM connecting sales, project delivery, and finance.

The choice to build internally

The team had tried Salesforce, but its structure required workarounds around our existing process. The alternatives were to keep adapting it, change our process to fit it, or build internally. We chose an internal CRM around the sales, delivery, and finance handoffs.

That choice gives us control over the handoffs, but also means owning development, deployment, and support. An established CRM can be the better option when its process fits the business.

I look at the workflow from the viewpoint of the people using the CRM. I map requirements around what sales, delivery, and finance need before they can act: the approved scope, supporting documents, current status, and the person responsible for the next step.

From lead to sales order

A qualified lead becomes an account, a contact, and an opportunity. One account can have several opportunities, each with its own sales funnel and approval requirements.

When an opportunity is won, the approved quotation becomes a numbered sales order. The order links the sale to a project with its items, budget, team, phases, and milestones.

From delivery to payment

Each project phase has deliverables and a progress percentage. Once a phase is complete, the team submits a milestone claim with evidence. Management approves it before finance issues the invoice.

The same records need to show delivery progress, billed amounts, receipts, and outstanding payments. Otherwise, finance and delivery have to reconstruct the status separately.

Customer receipts and supplier costs

On the customer side, a milestone claim becomes a sales invoice, then a receipt matched to the invoice. The accounting entry goes to Autocount with its supporting documents.

On the supplier side, a purchase order links to the sales order. Finance matches the supplier invoice to that purchase order, approves a payment voucher, and posts the cost to the project.

My role

I work across requirements, design, development, production deployment, and support. I clarify who owns each record, what a status means, and what happens when scope changes or an approval arrives late.

For a milestone claim, that means defining the evidence and management approval finance needs before issuing an invoice. I work through ownership and approval conditions before adding fields or screens. Support can reveal gaps, such as an incomplete claim or a late handover.

The internal CRM is still in progress. Client-specific implementation details and operational results remain confidential.

entry.title: A Web3 Payment Needs More Than a Transaction Hash
entry.content:
A transaction hash identifies a submitted transaction. The backend still needs to confirm what happened before crediting a ledger or releasing an order.

While working on a multi-chain gateway, I kept returning to when each person can act on a payment state.

What each state needs to tell us

  • The customer needs to know whether to wait or retry.
  • The merchant needs to know whether to release the order.
  • The backend needs verified evidence before updating the ledger.
  • QA needs acceptance criteria for each transition.

Submission, confirmation, failure, and settlement need distinct meanings in the interface, webhook handler, and support process.

Detection and settlement

Client-side detection provides quick feedback when funds appear. Settlement requires a verified server-side signal, with checks for the network, token, recipient, amount, transaction status, and duplicate processing.

Acceptance criteria I would write

  • Give each payment request a unique reference and expiry.
  • Check the selected token and network before signing.
  • Record the transaction hash without marking it settled.
  • Define separate responses for delays, failures, and duplicates.
  • Verify a webhook before it updates the ledger.
  • Prevent retries from crediting the same payment twice.

The CryptoRails lifecycle note covers the documented deposit and consolidation flow. These are generalised requirements; internal details and performance results remain confidential.

Related reading

  • Deposit detection, consolidation, and settlement in CryptoRails.
  • How I define when a payment is complete.

entry.title: A Small Talk About Hackathons
entry.content:
The time and energy hackathons demand is insane. Preliminary rounds, semi-finals, and finals each mean another round of brainstorming, last-minute changes, and almost no sleep.

At first, I finished each one looking forward to the next. After enough rounds, I was tired before the next competition started.

I also kept comparing myself to people who work in tech every day. I’m a mathematics student exploring outside my field, but that’s easy to forget when everyone around me seems more experienced.

There’s one more hackathon coming up. I’ll give it what I can, then take a proper break. I still want to do hackathons, but I need time away from the constant cycle of proving myself.

entry.title: Dead Internet Theory #1
entry.content:
LinkedIn and Reddit have started to feel different. I keep seeing polished posts that say the right things but feel disconnected from a person. I’m unsure whether that’s a real shift or my own overreaction.

I used ChatGPT to help write content in the past. Reading it back, I could tell it didn’t sound like anything I had experienced. The sentences were clean; the experience felt artificial.

Chatbots are useful for proofreading, restructuring, and catching the sentence I somehow wrote twice. They should not supply the experience itself. I would rather read a long-ass, badly organised article by someone who was there than a perfect post assembled from general opinions.

I can’t tell whether I’m seeing more bots, more generated content, or becoming more sensitive to both. If you’ve noticed it too, email me.

entry.title: Building a DeepSeek-R1 Chatbot
entry.content:
I built a chatbot with DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B to experiment with a downloadable reasoning model. The interface separates its intermediate output from the final response.

Try the Hugging Face demo or read the source.

Showing the intermediate output

While testing responses, I noticed the model produced reasoning text before its answer. I decided to display it rather than discard it.

Asked about climate change in Malaysia, it produced a structured response but included the Andaman and Nicobar Islands and a “Ch bamboo” initiative I had never heard of. The output sounded convincing despite those mistakes.

Showing the intermediate text helped me inspect the response and compare prompts. It still needed fact-checking.

Hosting the experiment

I used Gradio on a basic Hugging Face Spaces instance with 2 vCPUs and 16 GB RAM. That limits inference speed; the demo can take time to respond.

The small model made the experiment manageable. I could download it, inspect the model card, and change the interface without depending on a paid inference API.

For model details and published results, see the official model card. The Spaces documentation covers hosting.

entry.title: Eco Finance: A PayHack Prototype
entry.content:
We built Eco Finance during PayHack 2024 to show estimated carbon emissions alongside everyday spending. It was a 24-hour prototype using OpenFinance transaction data and dummy emission factors.

Estimating a transaction’s footprint

The proposed calculation uses the merchant category code (MCC), an emission factor, and the amount spent. For example, a dummy factor of 0.5 kg CO₂ per RM gives an estimate of 50 kg CO₂ for a RM 100 transaction.

Real use would require research into the factors for each merchant category. We considered surveys and work with DOSM; the hackathon version did not validate those estimates.

The proposed business model

We explored pooling users’ estimated savings, certifying carbon credits, selling them to companies, and rewarding users. Bursa Carbon Exchange was the market reference. This was a proposal to investigate, not an implemented or validated credit system.

What we built

We made a customer interface and an admin view. The demo is no longer maintained, so these screenshots record the prototype.

We didn’t make the final round T.T. I wrote more about the build, mentoring, and deadline problems in my first hackathon experience.

entry.title: First Physical Hackathon Experience
entry.content:
Janice, Roius, Gwyn, and I entered PayHack 2024 as four mathematics students from UTAR. Only two of us had tried a hackathon; Gwyn had never written code. None of us had much web development experience.

We made the Top 32 from almost 100 teams. Then we had four days to learn enough Vue.js and Flask to build a prototype while juggling internships. Janice travelled from JB to KL for it.

The idea and the questions we hadn’t answered

Our idea estimated carbon footprints from transaction data and explored pooling the savings for trading.

Johan Nasir’s mentoring sessions felt like a rotan session. “What happens if the carbon credits are manipulated?” “How do you ensure the authenticity of the footprint data?” Each question sent us back to the assumptions behind the demo.

Keeping the demo alive

We worked through tutorials after our internships. At the hackathon, we took turns sleeping. I couldn’t get a tent, so I used a bench for four-hour naps.

At 8:30 AM on submission day, 90 minutes before the deadline, our backend crashed while parsing information. We hardcoded some components to submit by 10 AM.

The pitch

We didn’t make the Top 10. A blockchain remittance team stood out because they had researched regulation and validated their market as carefully as they had built the product.

The stronger pitches connected features to business problems, survived the demo pressure, and answered questions with numbers. Next time, I wanted to validate the market earlier and practise the pitch more.

I did win a Samsung monitor in the lucky draw. That gave our tired team something to laugh about.

Janice, Roius, and Gwyn took the risk with me. Johan kept asking the questions we wanted to avoid. PayNet and JomHack gave us a place to build and test an idea outside the classroom.
